android_only_features:
ANDROID-ONLY features (NO desktop equivalent):

1. AetherVpnService (service/AetherVpnService.kt) — Full Android VPN service using android.net.VpnService API: creates TUN interface via ParcelFileDescriptor, manages VPN lifecycle (start/stop/restart), foreground service with notifications, wake lock management, network callbacks for connectivity changes, auto-reconnect on network loss, statistics collection via HevTun2SocksEngine or SocksTunBridge. Desktop has NO VPN service — it uses TunHelper with a PowerShell helper script and Wintun/TAP adapter instead.

2. AetherProxyService (service/AetherProxyService.kt) — Android foreground service for proxy-only mode (no VPN tunnel). Runs ConnectionController in a persistent service with wake lock, notifications, and widget updates. Desktop equivalent is just a local SOCKS/HTTP proxy server (LocalSocksProxyServer/LocalHttpProxyServer) running as regular threads within the app process, not a system service.

3. AetherTileService (service/AetherTileService.kt) — Android Quick Settings tile for one-tap connect/disconnect from notification shade. Uses android.service.quicksettings.TileService. No desktop equivalent (desktop uses system tray instead).

4. AetherWidgetProvider (service/AetherWidgetProvider.kt) — Android home screen widget showing connection status with protocol selector buttons (MASQUE, WireGuard, Gool) and toggle button. Uses AppWidgetProvider/RemoteViews. No desktop equivalent.

5. HevTun2SocksEngine (core/HevTun2SocksEngine.kt) — Wraps HevTun2SocksNative JNI calls to run hev-tun2socks as a native event loop on Android. Manages TUN file descriptor lifecycle via ParcelFileDescriptor, start/stop/pause/resume, upstream updates, statistics collection. Desktop uses TunHelper (heavily different approach: PowerShell scripts + external hev-socks5-tunnel.exe process + Wintun adapter).

6. HevTun2SocksNative (core/HevTun2SocksNative.kt) — JNI bindings loading 'hev-tun2socks-jni' native library via System.loadLibrary. External functions: nativeStart, nativeStop, nativePause, nativeResume, nativeUpdateUpstream, nativeGetStats, nativeGetVersion. Desktop has NO JNI — uses external process execution instead.

7. HevTun2SocksConfig (core/HevTun2SocksConfig.kt) — Generates YAML configuration string for the native hev-tun2socks engine (MTU, SOCKS5 address, UDP mode, mapdns, NAT64 prefix, timeouts, max sessions). Desktop TunHelper builds its own YAML config differently for the exe version.

8. SocksTunBridge (core/SocksTunBridge.kt) — Pure-Kotlin fallback SOCKS-to-TUN bridge for Android when hev-tun2socks native library is unavailable. Reads raw IP packets from TUN fd, parses IP headers, extracts TCP/UDP flow keys (FlowKey4/FlowKey6), connects to SOCKS5 proxy, handles UDP relay, DNS interception via DnsMap, RoutingEngine integration. 1688 lines. Desktop has NO equivalent — it relies entirely on the external hev-socks5-tunnel.exe.

9. CloakNative (core/CloakNative.kt — Android version) — JNI bindings loading 'cloak' native library. External functions: start, stop, isRunning, setLogLevel. Desktop CloakNative is a thin wrapper that delegates to CloakController (no JNI).

10. CloakController (core/CloakController.kt — Android version) — Manages Cloak obfuscation server via System.loadLibrary('cloak') JNI. Generates cloak.conf, manages process lifecycle via JNI calls. Desktop CloakController uses an external binary process (CloakController.desktop.kt) OR CloakEmbeddedServer (pure-Kotlin TLS SNI imitation fallback).

11. CloakEmbeddedServer (desktop only but relevant comparison) — Desktop has this as a pure-Kotlin fallback that mimics TLS handshakes to fool DPI. Android does NOT have this — it relies on the native cloak library.

12. PsiphonController (core/PsiphonController.kt) — Integrates Psiphon circumvention library via reflection (Class.forName('ca.psiphon.PsiphonTunnel')). Handles VPN service binding for socket protection, SOCKS5 port management, egress region discovery, connection state callbacks. Desktop has NO Psiphon integration at all.

13. ConnectionOwnerResolver (core/ConnectionOwnerResolver.kt) — Android-only: resolves which app (UID) owns a network connection. Uses ConnectivityManager.getConnectionOwnerUid() on API 29+, falls back to parsing /proc/net/tcp and /proc/net/tcp6. Required for per-app split tunneling on Android. Desktop doesn't need this — it uses system proxy settings.

14. DirectRouteVerifier (core/DirectRouteVerifier.kt) — Verifies that domain requests bypass the tunnel by checking exit IP via ipwho.is and ip-api.com APIs using Android's Network object for direct (non-tunneled) connectivity. Desktop has no equivalent — the RoutingEngine handles bypass at the proxy level.

15. LocalDnsResolver (core/LocalDnsResolver.kt) — Android DNS resolver that forwards DNS queries through SOCKS5 proxy (via VPN-protected sockets) with direct DNS fallback. Uses VpnService.protect() to prevent routing loops. Desktop equivalent is LocalDnsServer which is a full DNS server (UDP+TCP) with different architecture.

16. BinaryManager (core/BinaryManager.kt — Android version) — Detects device architecture via Build.SUPPORTED_ABIS, manages binary extraction from nativeLibraryDir (libaether.so), makes binaries executable. Desktop BinaryManager.desktop.kt handles x86/x86_64 binary preparation differently.

17. AetherProcessRunner (core/AetherProcessRunner.kt — app/src version) — Android-specific: launches aether_core binary with Android-specific environment variables, manages smart reconnection with exponential backoff, quick retry after cached gateway loss, stability checks. Desktop has its own AetherProcessRunner in commonMain with platform differences.

18. AetherRegistrationRunner (core/AetherRegistrationRunner.kt) — Runs protocol registration/test via external binary with Android context. Uses ProcessBuilder to execute binary with protocol-specific flags. Desktop commonMain has an equivalent.

19. NetworkClient (core/NetworkClient.kt) — Android-only: OkHttpClient singleton with 10s timeouts. Desktop uses its own HTTP client setup.

20. LocalSocksProxyServer (core/LocalSocksProxyServer.kt — Android version) — Android SOCKS5 proxy server with VPN socket protection, SOCKS5 handshake, routing engine integration, DnsMap lookups. Desktop has equivalent LocalSocksProxyServer without VPN dependencies.

21. RoutingEngine (core/RoutingEngine.kt — Android version) — Includes PORT and PRIVATE match types that desktop version lacks. Android version also matches on destinationPort and private networks directly. Desktop version has same core but fewer match types.

22. DnsMap (core/DnsMap.kt) — Shared between both platforms (exists in both). IP-to-domain cache with TTL expiry.

23. TrafficSniffer (core/TrafficSniffer.kt) — Shared between both platforms. TLS SNI and HTTP Host header extraction.

24. AndroidManifest.xml — Declares all Android services, permissions (INTERNET, WAKE_LOCK, FOREGROUND_SERVICE, QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES, etc.), widget configuration, tile service, network security config.

25. Android.mk, Application.mk — Android NDK build files for native library compilation.

26. ConnectionController (core/ConnectionController.kt — app/src version) — The full Android ConnectionController with TrafficStats-based traffic monitoring, broadcast-based status changes, per-app UID tracking, split tunneling via blocked packages. Desktop version is simpler.
desktop_only_features:
DESKTOP-ONLY features (NO Android equivalent):

1. TunHelper (core/TunHelper.kt) — Windows-specific TUN adapter management using PowerShell scripts + Wintun/TAP adapter. Creates virtual network interface 'AetherST', configures IP routes, manages hev-socks5-tunnel.exe as external process. Requires UAC elevation. Android uses VPN API instead.

2. Elevation (core/Elevation.kt) — Windows UAC elevation detection (net session) and app relaunch-as-admin via PowerShell Start-Process -Verb RunAs. Android has no equivalent (uses VPN permission prompt instead).

3. NetworkHealer (core/NetworkHealer.kt) — Windows-only: cleans up stale virtual routes, strips orphan TAP/Wintun adapter IPs, kills orphan PowerShell helper processes, resets adapter DNS, flushes DNS cache. Critical for clean shutdown. Android doesn't need this.

4. SingleInstanceLock (core/SingleInstanceLock.kt) — Prevents multiple desktop instances via ServerSocket lock on port 18195. Android handles this via Activity lifecycle.

5. AetherTray (desktop/AetherTray.kt) — System tray icon with custom Swing popup menu, connection toggle, status display, open settings/routing/logs actions. Desktop equivalent of Android's TileService + Widget.

6. RenderCompat (desktop/RenderCompat.kt) — GPU rendering detection and software fallback. Detects Intel HD Graphics issues, checks OpenGL capabilities, manages relaunch with different rendering backends (hardware vs software). Android handles this automatically.

7. UninstallCleanup (platform/UninstallCleanup.kt) — Windows-specific: tracks installation state, cleans up AppData directory on uninstall, detects orphaned installations.

8. DesktopLogger (shared/desktop/DesktopLogger.kt) — Desktop file-based logging with log rotation, fallback file logging, structured log entries. Android uses LogRepository + Android logging.

9. LocalHttpProxyServer (core/LocalHttpProxyServer.kt) — Desktop HTTP proxy server with CONNECT tunneling support. Android doesn't have a separate HTTP proxy server.

10. LocalDnsServer (core/LocalDnsServer.kt) — Desktop full DNS server (UDP + TCP) with upstream forwarding, DNS caching, TTL management. Android uses simpler LocalDnsResolver.

11. CloakEmbeddedServer (core/CloakEmbeddedServer.kt) — Pure-Kotlin Cloak implementation for desktop that mimics TLS SNI handshakes, handles fragmentation, jitter. Fallback when native Cloak binary unavailable. Android has no equivalent.

12. main.kt — Desktop application entry point with RenderCompat initialization, single instance lock, window setup.

13. Platform.desktop.kt — Desktop platform detection (OS, arch), window title, platform-specific utility functions.

14. Settings.desktop.kt — Desktop settings persistence (file-based vs Android SharedPreferences).

15. BinaryManager.desktop.kt — Desktop binary preparation (x86/x86_64), different architecture detection (OS arch vs Android ABIs).

16. PlatformProcess.desktop.kt — Desktop process management (different from Android's Process API).

17. PlatformComponents.desktop.kt — Desktop-specific UI components.

18. FlagImage.desktop.kt — Desktop flag image loading.

19. RenderCompat (GPU detection, software rendering fallback for incompatible hardware).
shared_features:
SHARED features (exist in both Android and Desktop):

1. ConnectionController — Both have ConnectionController (Android: full implementation with traffic stats, broadcasts; Desktop: uses Bridge pattern with status/traffic/elapsed overrides). Both manage connection lifecycle.

2. AetherProcessRunner — Both launch external aether_core binary. Common interface with platform-specific execution.

3. AetherRegistrationRunner — Both run protocol registration/test via external binary.

4. RoutingEngine — Both implement rule-based routing (domain, IP, keyword, regex, CIDR matching). Desktop version lacks PORT and PRIVATE match types.

5. DnsMap — Both have identical IP-to-domain cache with TTL expiry.

6. TrafficSniffer — Both have identical TLS SNI and HTTP Host header extraction.

7. CloakController — Both manage Cloak obfuscation config generation and lifecycle. Android uses JNI, Desktop uses external process or embedded server.

8. CloakNative — Both have CloakNative wrapper (Android: JNI calls, Desktop: delegates to CloakController).

9. BinaryManager — Both prepare platform-specific binaries. Different architecture detection.

10. PlatformProcess — Both manage external process execution. Different APIs.

11. LocalSocksProxyServer — Both run local SOCKS5 proxy server. Android version has VPN socket protection.

12. Platform — Both have platform detection and utilities.

13. Settings — Both persist settings. Different storage backends.

14. PlatformComponents — Both have platform-specific UI components.

15. FlagImage — Both load flag images. Different implementations.

16. ConnectionController (composeApp) — Both have the common/actual pattern for connection status.

17. AetherConfig, ConnectionStatus, SessionTraffic — Shared data models.

18. AetherConfigRepository — Shared configuration management.

19. LogRepository — Shared logging abstraction.

20. ActiveProxyProvider — Shared proxy state management.

21. Bridge — Shared platform bridge for status/traffic/elapsed overrides.
key_differences:
KEY DIFFERENCES IN IMPLEMENTATION APPROACH:

1. VPN/TUN MANAGEMENT: Android uses system VPN API (android.net.VpnService) with ParcelFileDescriptor for TUN interface. Desktop uses Wintun/TAP adapter via PowerShell scripts requiring UAC elevation. Android is simpler (one permission dialog), Desktop requires admin rights.

2. NATIVE LIBRARIES: Android uses JNI (System.loadLibrary) for hev-tun2socks and Cloak. Desktop uses external processes (.exe files) with no JNI. Desktop has pure-Kotlin fallback (CloakEmbeddedServer) when native libs unavailable.

3. PROCESS MANAGEMENT: Android manages processes within the app sandbox with VpnService protection. Desktop uses ProcessBuilder with PowerShell elevation and system-level route manipulation.

4. APP-LEVEL ROUTING: Android has ConnectionOwnerResolver (per-app UID via /proc/net) for split tunneling. Desktop uses system proxy settings and RoutingEngine rules without per-app control.

5. CIRCUMVENTION: Android has Psiphon integration (reflection-based JNI loading). Desktop has no Psiphon. Both have Cloak, but implementations differ (JNI vs external process).

6. SYSTEM INTEGRATION: Android uses Quick Settings Tile + Home Screen Widget. Desktop uses System Tray icon with Swing popup menu.

7. NETWORK HEALING: Desktop has NetworkHealer for cleanup (stale routes, orphan adapters). Android relies on VPN service lifecycle for cleanup.

8. DNS RESOLUTION: Android uses LocalDnsResolver (simple SOCKS5 forwarding with VPN protection). Desktop uses LocalDnsServer (full DNS server with UDP+TCP, caching, upstream forwarding).

9. TRAFFIC MONITORING: Android uses Android TrafficStats API. Desktop uses ProcessHandle and system-level monitoring.

10. ERROR RECOVERY: Desktop has Elevation.relaunchElevatedAndExit() for UAC elevation. Android relies on VPN permission prompts and foreground service restart.
porting_difficulty:
PORTING DIFFICULTY ASSESSMENT:

CRITICAL (High effort, requires fundamental rearchitecture):
- AetherVpnService → Desktop has NO equivalent. Desktop uses TunHelper+PowerShell+Wintun. Porting VPN-style tunnel management to desktop requires either maintaining the current approach or creating a cross-platform TUN abstraction.
- HevTun2SocksNative/Engine → Desktop uses external process, not JNI. Would need JNI compilation for desktop or maintain process-based approach.
- SocksTunBridge → 1688-line pure-Kotlin TUN bridge. Desktop doesn't need it (uses hev-socks5-tunnel.exe). Could be useful as fallback.
- PsiphonController → Desktop has NO Psiphon integration. Would require JNI library for desktop platforms.

MEDIUM (Platform API differences, straightforward adaptation):
- ConnectionOwnerResolver → Not needed on desktop (no per-app routing).
- DirectRouteVerifier → Not needed (RoutingEngine handles bypass).
- LocalDnsResolver → Desktop has LocalDnsServer (different but equivalent).
- BinaryManager → Different arch detection, similar logic.
- AetherProcessRunner → Common interface, platform-specific execution.

LOW (Simple wrapper differences):
- CloakNative → Desktop already has wrapper.
- CloakController → Desktop already has implementation.
- DnsMap, TrafficSniffer → Already shared/identical.
- PlatformComponents, FlagImage → Already have desktop implementations.

NOT NEEDED on Desktop:
- AetherTileService (Quick Settings tile is Android-only)
- AetherWidgetProvider (Home screen widget is Android-only)
- AetherProxyService (Desktop uses in-process proxy servers)
- AndroidManifest.xml, Android.mk, Application.mk

OVERALL: The desktop version already has most core functionality ported. The main gaps are: (1) No Psiphon support, (2) Different TUN implementation approach (PowerShell vs JNI), (3) No per-app routing capability. The architecture is well-factored with platform-specific source sets.
